rows.question: Does the technical documentation of a high-risk AI system require to provide specifications regarding the required hardware?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 11, a provider must draw up technical documentation containing the information set out in Annex IV, which expressly requires a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV point 1(e)) and, as part of the system's development description, the computational resources used to develop, train, test and validate it (Annex IV point 2(c)).
criteria_text: Yes
Description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run (Annex IV.1.e)
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'Yes' as the position, which matches the required verdict in criterion 1.

The answer explicitly states that the technical documentation must include 'a description of the hardware on which the AI system is intended to run', citing Annex IV point 1(e), which conveys the substance of the requirement.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and coherent prose suitable for regulatory advice.

rows.question: I have a medical device that has an AI system as a safety component. The medical device is classified "medium-risk" and undergoes a 3rd party conformity assessment. Is the AI system "medium risk" too? If yes, why? If not, why not?
rows.answer: No. The AI system is high-risk under the AI Act; "medium-risk" is a Medical Device Regulation classification and has no counterpart in Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, which does not operate a medium-risk tier for AI systems. Under Article 6(1) an AI system is high-risk where both conditions are met cumulatively: (a) it is intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or is itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I; and (b) that product is required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service under that legislation. The operator's device is covered by Regulation (EU) 2017/745, listed at Annex I, point 11, and its MDR class requires notified-body involvement, so both limbs are satisfied and the classification follows automatically, the device's own risk class affects only whether limb (b) is triggered, not the AI grading. The Article 6(3) derogation is unavailable, as it applies solely to Annex III systems. Consequently, Chapter III, Section 2 requirements apply, assessed within the MDR notified-body procedure under Article 43(3), with points 4.3, 4.4, 4.5 and the fifth paragraph of point 4.6 of Annex VII also applying.
criteria_text: Yes - high-risk (AI Act has no "medium-risk" category)
Condition (a): AI system is safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation (medical devices under Regulation (EU) 2017/745)
Condition (b): that product is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment
Both conditions cumulative under Article 6(1), irrespective of the device's own sectoral risk classification
criterion_remarks: Answer correctly states that the AI system is high-risk and that 'medium-risk' is not a category under the AI Act.
Answer identifies that the AI system is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation (specifically Regulation (EU) 2017/745).
Answer confirms the product requires third-party conformity assessment via notified-body involvement.
Answer explains that both conditions under Article 6(1) are cumulative and that the sectoral risk classification does not affect the AI system's high-risk status.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose suitable for regulatory compliance use.

rows.question: We want to deploy an AI system that performs biometric verification solely to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be. Is this system prohibited? Is it high-risk?
rows.answer: No, the system is not prohibited, and on these facts it is not high-risk. Article 5(1) lists no prohibited practice covering one-to-one biometric verification; the prohibition in Article 5(1)(g) concerns biometric categorisation to infer sensitive attributes, not identity confirmation. Annex III, point 1(a) covers remote biometric identification systems but expressly excludes AI systems intended to be used for biometric verification whose sole purpose is to confirm that a specific natural person is the person he or she claims to be, so Article 6(2) is not triggered unless the system also falls under another Annex III use case.
criteria_text: No, not prohibited
No, not high-risk
Falls within Annex III.1(a) biometric verification exclusion
criterion_remarks: The answer states the system is not prohibited, correctly noting that Article 5(1) does not prohibit one-to-one biometric verification and distinguishing the prohibited practice in Article 5(1)(g).

The answer explicitly states the system is not high-risk and explains that Annex III.1(a) does not trigger Article 6(2) high-risk classification due to the exclusion for biometric verification for identity confirmation.
The answer cites the exclusion in Annex III.1(a) for biometric verification systems whose sole purpose is confirming identity, matching the substance of the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents regulatory analysis suitable for compliance use.

rows.question: Which article of the EU AI Act governs human oversight measures?
rows.answer: Human oversight is governed by Article 14 of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. It requires that high-risk AI systems be designed and developed, including through appropriate human-machine interface tools, so that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons while in use (Article 14(1)), with oversight aimed at preventing or minimising risks to health, safety or fundamental rights arising from intended use or reasonably foreseeable misuse (Article 14(2)). Measures must be commensurate with the risks, level of autonomy and context of use, and delivered either as measures built into the system by the provider or as measures identified by the provider for the deployer to implement (Article 14(3)(a), (b)). Article 14(4) specifies the capabilities to be enabled, understanding capacities and limitations, awareness of automation bias, correct interpretation of output, deciding not to use or to disregard, override or reverse output, and intervening or stopping the system, and Article 14(5) adds separate verification by at least two competent natural persons for Annex III point 1(a) remote biometric identification systems, save where Union or national law deems this disproportionate for law enforcement, migration, border control or asylum.
criteria_text: Article 14
Design for effective human oversight during use
Aim: prevent/minimise risks to health, safety, fundamental rights
Measures built in by provider and/or implemented by deployer
Overseers enabled to understand, monitor, interpret, override, and halt the system
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that human oversight is governed by Article 14.
The answer states that high-risk AI systems must be designed and developed so they can be effectively overseen during use, capturing the substance of Article 14(1).
The answer specifies that oversight aims to prevent or minimise risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights from intended use or foreseeable misuse, reflecting Article 14(2).
The answer describes that measures may be built into the system by the provider or implemented by the deployer, in line with Article 14(3)(a) and (b).

The answer lists all five capabilities from Article 14(4): understanding capacities and limitations, awareness of automation bias, correct interpretation, ability to override or reverse output, and ability to intervene or stop the system.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents information in a logical, actionable manner.

rows.question: Under what conditions should providers of general-purpose AI models be subject to exceptions regarding transparency-related requirements, if any? And what do those exceptions not cover?
rows.answer: The exceptions to the GPAI transparency-related obligations are set out in Article 53(2). The Article 53(1)(a) duty to draw up and keep up-to-date the technical documentation of the model (Annex XI) and the Article 53(1)(b) duty to provide information and documentation to downstream providers (Annex XII) do not apply to providers that release the model under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution, where the model parameters, including the weights, and information on the model architecture and usage, are made publicly available. The exception does not cover the remaining Article 53(1) obligations: the policy to comply with Union copyright law (Article 53(1)(c)) and the publicly available, sufficiently detailed summary of the training content (Article 53(1)(d)) apply regardless of the licence. The exception also does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk (Article 53(2), second subparagraph), which remain subject to the full Article 53 obligations together with the Article 55 systemic-risk duties.
criteria_text: Yes, exceptions exist
Condition: model released under free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification and distribution
Condition: parameters (weights, architecture info, usage info) made publicly available
Exception covers only points (a) and (b) of Article 53(1), not (c)/(d)
Exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk
criterion_remarks: The answer affirms the existence of exceptions in Article 53(2).
The answer states the model must be released under a free and open-source licence allowing access, usage, modification, and distribution.
The answer specifies that parameters, including weights, architecture, and usage information, must be made publicly available.
The answer clearly limits the exception to points (a) and (b) of Article 53(1), and explicitly states that (c) and (d) still apply.
The answer states the exception does not apply to general-purpose AI models with systemic risk, which remain subject to full obligations.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; presents information in a coherent, regulatory-appropriate manner without self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: What are the administrative fines for non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices?
rows.answer: Non-compliance with the prohibition of the AI practices in Article 5 is subject to the Regulation's highest penalty tier: administrative fines of up to EUR 35 000 000 or, if the offender is an undertaking, up to 7 % of its total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher (Article 99(3)). The ceiling applies to any of the eight prohibited practices listed in Article 5(1), points (a) to (h), and attaches to placing on the market, putting into service or use, whoever the operator is. For SMEs, including start-ups, the same ceilings apply but up to the percentage or the amount referred to in Article 99(3), whichever is lower (Article 99(6)). The fine must in each case be effective, proportionate and dissuasive, with Member States laying down the rules on penalties and taking into account the criteria in Article 99(1) and (7). Article 5 breaches are expressly carved out of the lower EUR 15 000 000 / 3 % tier, which covers only the operator and notified-body provisions listed in Article 99(4), points (a) to (g).
criteria_text: EUR 35,000,000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher
Applies to non-compliance with Article 5 prohibited AI practices
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states the fine amount as EUR 35,000,000 or 7% of total worldwide annual turnover for the preceding financial year, whichever is higher, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The candidate answer explicitly links the fine to non-compliance with the prohibition of AI practices in Article 5, satisfying the substance of criterion 2.

rows.question: What is a deep fake according to the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: ‘deep fake’ means AI-generated or manipulated image, audio or video content that resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events and would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful;
criteria_text: AI-generated or manipulated content
Image, audio, or video
Resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events
Falsely appears authentic or truthful to a person
criterion_remarks: The answer states that deep fakes are AI-generated or manipulated content, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The answer specifies image, audio or video content, which matches the substance of criterion 2.
The answer includes that the content resembles existing persons, objects, places, entities or events, which matches the substance of criterion 3.
The answer states the content would falsely appear to a person to be authentic or truthful, which matches the substance of criterion 4.
rows.tone_remark: The response is in neutral, professional language, directly quoting the definition from the Act in a clear and concise manner suitable for a regulatory context.

rows.question: What are all the risk categories in the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: The EU AI Act sets four risk tiers plus a separate regime for general-purpose AI models: unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5; and high-risk systems are classified under Article 6 (an Annex I product safety component, or an Annex III use case) and carry the Chapter III Section 2 obligations. Limited-risk systems carry the Article 50 transparency duties, minimal-risk systems avoid Chapter III high-risk requirements but retain Article 4 AI literacy duties, with voluntary codes under Article 95, and general-purpose AI models are governed separately under Articles 51 to 56, with added obligations under Article 55 for models classified as having systemic risk under Article 51.
criteria_text: Unacceptable risk - prohibited practices (Article 5)
High risk - Article 6, referencing Annex I (product safety) and Annex III (use cases)
Limited risk - transparency obligations (Article 50)
Minimal or no risk - no mandatory obligations, voluntary codes of conduct (Article 95)
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that unacceptable-risk practices are prohibited under Article 5, conveying the substance of the criterion.
The answer identifies high-risk systems under Article 6 and references both Annex I (product safety) and Annex III (use cases), capturing the full substance of the criterion.
The answer states that limited-risk systems carry transparency duties under Article 50, which matches the substance of the criterion.
The answer notes that minimal-risk systems avoid high-risk obligations and mentions voluntary codes of conduct under Article 95, thereby stating the substance of the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured prose suitable for regulatory advice; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Can an operator that is not a provider according to the EU AI Act, for example a deployer, take actions on a given high-risk AI system such that it can be effectively seen as a provider by the authorities? If yes, what kind of action would result in such an outcome?
rows.answer: Yes. Under Article 25(1), a distributor, importer, deployer or other third party is deemed to be the provider of a high-risk AI system, and takes on the provider obligations in Article 16, in any of three cases. First, if it puts its name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already placed on the market (Article 25(1)(a)). Second, if it makes a substantial modification to a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk (Article 25(1)(b)). Third, if it modifies the intended purpose of an AI system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk (Article 25(1)(c)). In each of these three cases the operator assumes the provider obligations in Article 16, and the initial provider is no longer considered the provider of that specific system under Article 25(2).
criteria_text: Yes
Putting own name/trademark on a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service (Article 25(1)(a))
Substantial modification to a high-risk AI system already on the market/in service that remains high-risk under Article 6 (Article 25(1)(b))
Modifying the intended purpose of a non-high-risk (incl. general-purpose) AI system such that it becomes high-risk under Article 6 (Article 25(1)(c))
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states 'Yes' as its first word, clearly affirming the possibility.
The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(a) by explaining that putting one's name or trademark on a high-risk AI system already on the market results in being considered a provider.
The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(b) by describing substantial modification of a high-risk AI system that remains high-risk as a triggering condition.

The answer states the substance of Article 25(1)(c) by explaining that modifying the intended purpose of a non-high-risk system, including a general-purpose AI system, so that it becomes high-risk results in provider status.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and logical flow; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: According to Article 1, what is the objective of the EU AI Act?
rows.answer: The objective, under Article 1(1), is to improve the functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy artificial intelligence, while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection, against the harmful effects of AI systems in the Union, and supporting innovation. Article 1(2) implements that purpose through harmonised rules on placing on the market, putting into service and use of AI systems, prohibitions, high-risk requirements, transparency rules, general-purpose AI model rules, governance and enforcement, and innovation-support measures.
criteria_text: Improve functioning of the internal market
Promote uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI
Ensure high level of protection of health, safety and fundamental rights (incl. democracy, rule of law, environment) against harmful effects of AI systems
Support innovation
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that the objective includes improving the functioning of the internal market.
The answer explicitly states the objective of promoting the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy AI.
The answer includes the full scope of protection: health, safety, fundamental rights, democracy, rule of law, and environmental protection against harmful effects of AI systems.
The answer concludes with 'supporting innovation', which directly matches the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured prose that clearly conveys the regulatory purpose without self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Is an AI system used to structure or deduplicate information for a use case listed in Annex III considered high-risk?
rows.answer: No. Structuring or deduplicating information is a narrow procedural task, so the system falls under the Article 6(3) first subparagraph point (a) derogation and is not high-risk, provided it poses no significant risk of harm to health, safety or fundamental rights and does not materially influence the outcome of decision making; the other limbs are (b) improving the result of a previously completed human activity, (c) detecting decision-making patterns or deviations without replacing or influencing the human assessment, and (d) performing a preparatory task, and the derogation never applies where the system profiles natural persons. Under Article 6(4) a provider relying on the derogation must document the assessment before the system is placed on the market or put into service, and register it under Article 49(2).
criteria_text: No
Falls under narrow procedural task derogation, Article 6(3), first subparagraph, point (a)
Exception: remains high-risk if system performs profiling of natural persons
Provider must document the assessment before placing on market/putting into service (Article 6(4))
criterion_remarks: The answer states 'No' as the initial verdict, which matches the required 'No' in criterion 1 and is unambiguous.

The answer explicitly states that structuring or deduplicating information is a narrow procedural task and cites the correct provision, Article 6(3) first subparagraph point (a), satisfying the substance of the criterion.

The answer clearly excludes profiling of natural persons from the derogation by stating 'the derogation never applies where the system profiles natural persons', which captures the exception in the criterion.
The answer references Article 6(4) and states the provider must document the assessment before market placement or putting into service, which matches the requirement in the criterion.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what jurisdiction does the Court of Justice of the European Union have over Commission decisions fixing fines on providers of general-purpose AI models, and what can the Court do with the fine?
rows.answer: Under Article 101(5) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689, the Court of Justice of the European Union has unlimited jurisdiction to review decisions of the Commission fixing a fine under a full review on the merits of the amount, not merely a legality check. Exercising that jurisdiction, the Court may cancel, reduce or increase the fine imposed (Article 101(5)). The decisions so reviewable are those imposing fines on providers of general-purpose AI models of up to 3 % of annual total worldwide turnover in the preceding financial year or EUR 15 000 000, whichever is higher, for the intentional or negligent conduct listed in Article 101(1)(a), (d). In reviewing the amount, the Court applies the same statutory yardsticks that bind the Commission: nature, gravity and duration of the infringement, proportionality and appropriateness (Article 101(1)), and the requirement that fines be effective, proportionate and dissuasive (Article 101(3)).
criteria_text: Unlimited jurisdiction to review Commission decisions fixing a fine
Court may cancel the fine
Court may reduce the fine
Court may increase the fine
criterion_remarks: The answer states the Court has 'unlimited jurisdiction to review decisions of the Commission fixing a fine under a full review on the merits,' which conveys the substance of unlimited jurisdiction.
The answer explicitly states the Court 'may cancel, reduce or increase the fine imposed,' including 'cancel the fine.'
The answer includes 'reduce the fine' as one of the options the Court may exercise.
The answer explicitly states the Court 'may...increase the fine,' satisfying the criterion.

rows.question: When registering a high-risk AI system in the EU database under the EU AI Act, what specific information must the provider submit? List the required items.
rows.answer: Before placing an Annex III high-risk system on the market or putting it into service, the provider or authorised representative must register themselves and the system in the EU database (Article 49(1)), entering the Section A data of Annex VIII (Article 71(2)). The required items are: (1) the provider's name, address and contact details; (2) where another person submits on the provider's behalf, that person's name, address and contact details; (3) the authorised representative's name, address and contact details, where applicable; (4) the system's trade name and any additional unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability; (5) a description of the intended purpose and of the components and functions supported through the system; (6) a basic and concise description of the information used (data, inputs) and its operating logic; (7) the system's status (on the market, in service, no longer placed on the market or in service, recalled); (8) the type, number and expiry date of the notified body's certificate and that body's name or identification number, where applicable; (9) a scanned copy of that certificate; (10) the Member States where the system has been placed on the market, put into service or made available; (11) a copy of the EU declaration of conformity; (12) electronic instructions for use, which are not provided for law enforcement or migration, asylum and border-control systems under Annex III, points 1, 6 and 7; and (13) optionally, a URL for additional information.
criteria_text: Contact details of the provider, of any person submitting on its behalf and of the authorised representative, where applicable (Annex VIII, Section A, points 1 to 3)
AI system trade name and an unambiguous reference allowing identification and traceability (point 4)
Intended purpose and the components and functions the system supports (point 5)
Basic and concise description of the data and inputs used and the operating logic (point 6)
Market status and the notified body certificate details with a scanned copy, where applicable (points 7 to 9)
Member States concerned, a copy of the EU declaration of conformity and the electronic instructions for use (points 10 to 12)
criterion_remarks: The answer lists the provider's contact details, those of any person submitting on its behalf, and the authorised representative where applicable, satisfying the substance of point 1.
The answer includes the trade name and an unambiguous reference for identification and traceability as required by point 4.
The answer provides a description of the intended purpose and the components and functions supported by the system, matching point 5.
The answer states the requirement for a basic and concise description of the data, inputs, and operating logic, fulfilling point 6.
The answer includes the system's market status and all applicable certificate details with a scanned copy, covering points 7 to 9.
The answer lists the Member States concerned, a copy of the EU declaration of conformity, and electronic instructions for use, noting the exception, thus satisfying points 10 to 12.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral third-person register with clear structure and complete sentences; no self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, when a high-risk AI system is found to conform with the requirements, what information must the Union technical documentation assessment certificate contain?
rows.answer: Under Annex VII point 4.6, where the notified body finds the high-risk AI system conforms with the Chapter III Section 2 requirements, it issues a Union technical documentation assessment certificate. Per Annex VII point 4.6, that certificate must indicate the name and address of the provider, the conclusions of the examination, the conditions (if any) for its validity, and the data necessary for the identification of the AI system. Under Article 44(1) the certificate must be drawn up in a language which can be easily understood by the relevant authorities in the Member State in which the notified body is established, and under Article 44(2) it is valid for the period it indicates, which may not exceed five years for AI systems covered by Annex I and four years for AI systems covered by Annex III.
criteria_text: Language: drawn up in a language easily understood by the relevant authorities of the Member State where the notified body is established
Validity period stated: not exceeding five years (Annex I systems) or four years (Annex III systems)
criterion_remarks: The answer states the certificate must be drawn up in a language easily understood by the relevant authorities of the Member State where the notified body is established, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The answer specifies that the validity period may not exceed five years for Annex I systems and four years for Annex III systems, conveying the substance of criterion 2.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference or hedging; presents information in a coherent, actionable manner.

rows.question: Under Article 10(5) of the EU AI Act, when may a provider of a high-risk AI system process special categories of personal data for bias detection and correction, and what key safeguards/conditions must be met?
rows.answer: Under Article 10(5), a provider of a high-risk AI system may exceptionally process special categories of personal data only to the extent strictly necessary to ensure bias detection and correction, subject to appropriate safeguards. These conditions apply in addition to, and not instead of, Regulation (EU) 2016/679, Regulation (EU) 2018/1725 and Directive (EU) 2016/680. Article 10(5) requires all of the following: the bias work cannot be done with other data, including synthetic or anonymised data (a); technical limits on re-use plus state-of-the-art security and pseudonymisation (b); strict controls and documentation of access so that only authorised persons under appropriate confidentiality obligations can reach the data (c); the data are not transmitted, transferred or otherwise accessed by other parties (d); deletion once the bias is corrected or the retention period ends, whichever is first (e); and records of processing documenting why it was strictly necessary (f).
criteria_text: Only where strictly necessary for bias detection/correction under Art 10(2)(f)-(g), and cannot be effectively achieved with other data (incl. synthetic/anonymised)
Technical re-use limitations plus state-of-the-art security/privacy-preserving measures, including pseudonymisation
Strict, documented access controls limited to authorised persons under confidentiality obligations, with no transmission/transfer/access by other parties
Deletion once bias corrected or retention period ends, whichever is first
Processing records document necessity and why other data would not suffice
Additional to, not a substitute for, obligations under GDPR, EUDPR and the Law Enforcement Directive
criterion_remarks: Answer states processing is allowed only when strictly necessary and cannot be effectively fulfilled with other data, including synthetic or anonymised.
Answer includes technical limitations on re-use and specifies state-of-the-art security and pseudonymisation.
Answer covers strict, documented access controls limited to authorised persons under confidentiality obligations and prohibits transmission or access by others.
Answer explicitly states deletion upon bias correction or end of retention period, whichever comes first.
Answer notes that records must document the necessity and why other data types would not suffice.
Answer clarifies that the conditions are in addition to, not a substitute for, GDPR, EUDPR, and the Law Enforcement Directive.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; presents information in clear, coherent prose suitable for regulatory use.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must a provider of a high-risk AI system supply to the deployer in the instructions for use? List the required categories of information.
rows.answer: Under Article 13(3), a provider must accompany a high-risk AI system with concise, complete, correct and clear instructions for use covering at least six categories. First, the identity and contact details of the provider and, where applicable, its authorised representative (point (a)). Second, the system's characteristics, capabilities and limitations of performance (point (b)): its intended purpose; the level of accuracy, including metrics, robustness and cybersecurity under Article 15 against which it was tested and validated, plus circumstances affecting that level; known or foreseeable circumstances of intended use or reasonably foreseeable misuse that may risk health, safety or fundamental rights; where applicable, technical capabilities to explain its output; when appropriate, performance regarding specific persons or groups; when appropriate, input-data specifications or information on the training, validation and testing data sets; and, where applicable, information enabling deployers to interpret and appropriately use the output. Third, any changes to the system and its performance pre-determined by the provider at the initial conformity assessment (point (c)). Fourth, the human oversight measures under Article 14, including technical measures facilitating deployers' interpretation of outputs (point (d)). Fifth, the computational and hardware resources needed, the expected lifetime, and any necessary maintenance and care measures, including their frequency and software updates (point (e)). Sixth, where relevant, a description of the mechanisms allowing deployers to collect, store and interpret the logs in accordance with Article 12 (point (f)).
criteria_text: Provider and, where applicable, authorised representative identity/contact details

Characteristics, capabilities and performance limitations (intended purpose, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity levels, foreseeable risks, explainability capabilities, performance for specific groups, input data specifications)
Pre-determined changes to the system and its performance
Human oversight measures under Article 14
Computational/hardware resources needed, expected lifetime, and maintenance/care measures
Description of logging mechanisms under Article 12, where relevant
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states the provider and, where applicable, authorised representative identity and contact details as required by Article 13.3(a).

The answer comprehensively covers all sub-elements of Article 13.3(b), including intended purpose, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity, foreseeable risks, explainability capabilities, performance for specific groups, and input data specifications.
The answer clearly includes pre-determined changes to the system and its performance under Article 13.3(c).
The answer explicitly references human oversight measures under Article 14 and includes technical measures to facilitate interpretation of outputs as required by Article 13.3(d).
The answer includes computational and hardware resources, expected lifetime, and maintenance/care measures including frequency and software updates as required by Article 13.3(e).
The answer includes, where relevant, a description of mechanisms for log collection, storage and interpretation in accordance with Article 12 as required by Article 13.3(f).

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) Article 95, who may draw up codes of conduct, and which bodies must encourage and facilitate their drawing up?
rows.answer: Codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, by organisations representing them, or by both, while the AI Office and the Member States must encourage and facilitate their drawing up. Article 95(3) adds that drafting may involve any interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society organisations and academia, and that a code may cover one or more AI systems taking into account the similarity of their intended purpose. Article 95(1) places the duty to encourage and facilitate codes of conduct, including related governance mechanisms, on the AI Office and the Member States, for voluntary application to non-high-risk AI systems of some or all of the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements. Article 95(2) has those same bodies facilitate codes on voluntary application, including by deployers, of specific requirements to all AI systems. Article 95(4) requires them to take account of the specific interests and needs of SMEs, including start-ups. Annex VII, point 4(a), (c) concerns notified-body applications and bears on neither limb.
criteria_text: Codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers of AI systems, by organisations representing them, or both
May involve interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society and academia
The AI Office and the Member States must encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states that codes of conduct may be drawn up by individual providers or deployers, by organisations representing them, or by both, which matches the substance of criterion 1.

The candidate answer explicitly mentions that drafting may involve any interested stakeholders and their representative organisations, including civil society and academia, satisfying the substance of criterion 2.
The candidate answer clearly states that the AI Office and the Member States must encourage and facilitate the drawing up of codes of conduct, directly satisfying criterion 3.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what minimum elements must a provider's quality management system (QMS) for high-risk AI systems include? List the required elements.
rows.answer: Under Article 17(1), a provider of a high-risk AI system must put in place a quality management system ensuring compliance with the Regulation, documented in a systematic and orderly manner as written policies, procedures and instructions, and covering at least thirteen aspects. These are: (a) a strategy for regulatory compliance, including compliance with conformity assessment procedures and procedures for managing modifications to the system; (b) techniques, procedures and systematic actions for design, design control and design verification; (c) techniques, procedures and systematic actions for development, quality control and quality assurance; (d) examination, test and validation procedures before, during and after development, and their frequency; (e) technical specifications, including standards, and, where harmonised standards are not applied in full or do not cover all Chapter III, Section 2 requirements, the means used to ensure compliance; (f) systems and procedures for data management, covering acquisition, collection, analysis, labelling, storage, filtration, mining, aggregation and retention before and for the purpose of placing on the market; (g) the risk management system referred to in Article 9; (h) setting-up, implementation and maintenance of a post-market monitoring system under Article 72; (i) procedures for serious-incident reporting under Article 73; (j) handling of communication with national competent and other relevant authorities, notified bodies, other operators, customers and interested parties; (k) systems and procedures for record-keeping of all relevant documentation and information; (l) resource management, including security-of-supply measures; and (m) an accountability framework setting out the responsibilities of management and other staff for all those aspects. Implementation must be proportionate to the size of the provider's organisation, without lowering the rigour and level of protection needed for compliance (Article 17(2)). Providers already subject to quality-management obligations or an equivalent function under sectoral Union law may integrate these aspects into that system (Article 17(3)), and financial institutions subject to internal governance requirements under Union financial services law are deemed to satisfy the obligation by complying with those rules, except for points (g), (h) and (i) (Article 17(4)).
criteria_text: Regulatory compliance strategy incl. conformity assessment and modification management
Design, development, quality control and verification techniques/procedures
Examination, test and validation procedures and their frequency
Data management procedures across data lifecycle
Article 9 risk management system and Article 72 post-market monitoring system
Record-keeping and accountability framework for management/staff

The answer includes design, development, quality control, and verification techniques and procedures as required.

The answer details data management procedures across the data lifecycle, including acquisition, collection, labelling, storage, and retention.
The answer explicitly references the Article 9 risk management system and the Article 72 post-market monitoring system.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, in which specific situations may law enforcement use 'real-time' remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law-enforcement purposes (i.e., the exceptions to the prohibition)? List the permitted objectives.
rows.answer: Real‑time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law‑enforcement purposes is prohibited under Article 5(1)(h) unless and in so far as strictly necessary for one of three exhaustive objectives. First, Article 5(1)(h)(i): the targeted search for specific victims of abduction, trafficking in human beings or sexual exploitation of human beings, and the search for missing persons. Second, Article 5(1)(h)(ii): the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to the life or physical safety of natural persons, or of a genuine and present or genuine and foreseeable threat of a terrorist attack. Third, Article 5(1)(h)(iii): the localisation or identification of a person suspected of a criminal offence, for a criminal investigation, prosecution or execution of a criminal penalty, for offences listed in Annex II punishable in the Member State concerned by a custodial sentence or detention order of at least four years. Use is confined to confirming the identity of a specifically targeted individual and requires a completed fundamental rights impact assessment under Article 27 and registration of the system in the secure non‑public section of the EU database under Article 49(4), covering Annex VIII Section A points 1 to 10 except points 6, 8 and 9 (Article 49(4)(a)), Section B points 1 to 5 and 8 and 9 (Article 49(4)(b)), Section C points 1 to 3 (Article 49(4)(c)), and Annex IX points 1, 2, 3 and 5 (Article 49(4)(d)); in duly justified urgency, registration may follow without undue delay.
criteria_text: Targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, or missing persons
Prevention of specific, substantial and imminent threat to life/physical safety, or genuine terrorist attack threat
Localisation/identification of a suspect for investigation, prosecution, or executing a penalty for an Annex II offence punishable by at least 4 years custodial sentence/detention order
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states the targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking, sexual exploitation, and missing persons, which matches the substance of criterion 1.
The answer includes the prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety and of a genuine terrorist attack threat, capturing the substance of criterion 2.

The answer specifies the localisation or identification of a suspect for investigation, prosecution, or execution of a penalty for Annex II offences punishable by at least four years’ custodial sentence, which matches criterion 3.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what must providers of AI systems that generate or manipulate synthetic content do to enable identification of AI-generated/manipulated output, and what quality criteria must that solution meet?
rows.answer: Under Article 50, limited-risk transparency: AI systems interacting with natural persons must disclose AI nature; emotion-recognition and biometric-categorisation systems must inform exposed persons; deepfakes and AI-generated content must be labelled. Transparency obligations split by actor: providers must ensure AI systems interacting with natural persons disclose their AI nature (Article 50(1)) and must mark synthetic AI-generated content in a machine-readable, detectable format (Article 50(2)); deployers must inform exposed persons when operating emotion-recognition or biometric-categorisation systems (Article 50(3)) and must label deepfakes as artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(4)). For deepfakes forming part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work, transparency is limited to disclosure in an appropriate manner that does not hamper display or enjoyment of the work (Article 50(4) third subparagraph).
criteria_text: Marking must be machine-readable format
Marking must be detectable as artificially generated or manipulated
Solution must be effective, interoperable, robust and reliable, as far as technically feasible
Feasibility judged against content-type specificities/limitations, implementation costs, and state of the art
Exemptions: assistive editing, no substantial alteration of input data/semantics, or law-enforcement authorisation
criterion_remarks: The answer states that providers must mark synthetic AI-generated content in a machine-readable format, which conveys the substance of criterion 1.
The answer specifies that the marking must be detectable as artificially generated or manipulated, satisfying criterion 2.

The answer does not mention the quality criteria of effectiveness, interoperability, robustness, and reliability, nor does it state they must be met as far as technically feasible; thus, criterion 3 is not satisfied.
The answer omits any reference to how feasibility is assessed against content-type specificities, implementation costs, and state of the art, so criterion 4 is not satisfied.
The answer does not mention any of the three exemptions listed in the criterion (assistive editing, no substantial alteration, law-enforcement authorisation), so criterion 5 is not satisfied.
rows.tone_remark: The response uses professional, neutral, third-person language, is well-structured, and presents information in a coherent and actionable manner without self-reference or informality.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, which body has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce the obligations for providers of general-purpose AI models (Chapter V), and which entity is entrusted with implementing those tasks?
rows.answer: Under Article 53, GPAI providers must maintain Annex XI documentation, supply downstream-provider information, and publish a training-data summary; the Article 53(2) carve-out means each documentation obligation does not apply to free and open-source models below the systemic threshold. Under Article 51, a GPAI model has systemic risk when cumulative training compute exceeds 10²⁵ FLOPs (10^25); providers must notify the Commission within two weeks of meeting the threshold. Vests enforcement of the Chapter V obligations of providers of general-purpose AI models exclusively in the Commission, acting through the AI Office, which exercises the powers laid down in the Regulation without prejudice to the institutional powers set out in the Treaties (Article 88(1)).
criteria_text: European Commission has exclusive powers to supervise and enforce Chapter V
AI Office is entrusted with implementing these tasks
criterion_remarks: The answer states that enforcement of Chapter V obligations is vested exclusively in the Commission, which satisfies the substance of criterion 1.
The answer states that the Commission acts through the AI Office, which is entrusted with implementing the tasks, satisfying the substance of criterion 2.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral register; clear and coherent structure using full sentences without self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, what conditions must be met before data collected and processed for testing high-risk AI systems in real-world conditions can be transferred to a third country (outside the EU)?
rows.answer: Such data may be transferred outside the Union only where appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law are implemented; that is the sole transfer-specific condition, laid down in Article 60(4)(e) of Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. The condition is cumulative: it operates as one of the conditions in Article 60(4) that must all be met for testing in real world conditions to be lawful, alongside the submission and approval of the real-world testing plan by the market surveillance authority (Article 60(4)(a) and (b)), registration of the testing (Article 60(4)(c)), establishment or a legal representative in the Union (Article 60(4)(d)), and informed consent of the subjects of the testing (Article 60(4)(i)). Article 60 itself prescribes no further transfer mechanism; the "safeguards under Union law" are those of Union data protection law, which continue to apply in full, including to any special categories of personal data involved.
criteria_text: Appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law must be implemented for the transfer
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer explicitly states that appropriate and applicable safeguards under Union law must be implemented for the transfer, which matches the substance of the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; avoids self-reference, hedging, or informality while clearly conveying regulatory requirements.

rows.question: What are the conditions to classify general-purpose AI (GPAI) model as "GPAI model with systemic risk"? Do all need to be met at the same time?
rows.answer: No. The two conditions in Article 51(1) are alternatives, not cumulative: a general-purpose AI model is classified as one with systemic risk if it meets any of them. The first, Article 51(1)(a), is that the model has high impact capabilities, capabilities that match or exceed those recorded in the most advanced general-purpose AI models (Article 3(64)), evaluated on the basis of appropriate technical tools and methodologies, including indicators and benchmarks. The second, Article 51(1)(b), is a decision of the Commission, taken ex officio or following a qualified alert from the scientific panel, that the model has capabilities or an impact equivalent to those in point (a), having regard to the criteria in Annex XIII. Article 51(2) adds a rebuttable presumption, not a third condition: high impact capabilities under point (a) are presumed where the cumulative amount of computation used for training, measured in floating point operations, is greater than 10²⁵. Under Article 51(3) the Commission may amend those thresholds by delegated act. Classification triggers the Article 55 obligations in addition to Article 53.
criteria_text: Condition (a): high impact capabilities per Article 51(1)(a), presumed when training compute exceeds 10^25 FLOPs
Condition (b): Commission decision (ex officio or following qualified alert from scientific panel) that capabilities/impact are equivalent, per Annex XIII criteria
No, not cumulative - either condition alone suffices
criterion_remarks: The answer states the substance of the presumption based on training compute exceeding 10^25 FLOPs, citing Article 51(2).

The answer clearly explains that a Commission decision, ex officio or after a qualified alert, based on equivalence to high-impact capabilities using Annex XIII criteria, is sufficient for classification.
The answer explicitly states that the conditions are alternatives, not cumulative, and that either one suffices.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, is an AI system that is a safety component of a medical device classified as MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) automatically a high-risk AI system? Explain your reasoning.
rows.answer: No. Such a system is not automatically high-risk under the EU AI Act. Article 6(1)(a) is satisfied, since the AI system is a safety component of a product covered by Regulation (EU) 2017/745, listed in Annex I, point 11. But Article 6(1)(b) is not: a Class I device that is non-sterile, non-measuring and not a reusable surgical instrument is self-certified by the manufacturer without notified body involvement, so it is not required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment. Both conditions are cumulative. The system could still be high-risk under Article 6(2) if it falls within a listed Annex III use case.

Article 6(1)(a) and (b) are cumulative conditions
MDR Class I (non-sterile, non-measuring, non-reusable surgical) devices undergo manufacturer self-assessment, not third-party conformity assessment
Condition (b) fails, so Article 6(1) does not apply
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No' as the position, matching the required verdict.
The answer explicitly states that both conditions under Article 6(1) are cumulative, affirming the necessity of meeting both.
The answer correctly explains that MDR Class I devices of this type undergo self-assessment without notified body involvement, i.e., no third-party assessment.
The answer concludes that because condition (b) fails, Article 6(1) does not apply, directly addressing the logical consequence.

rows.question: Under the EU AI Act, can an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in a lift qualify as a high-risk AI system, and under what conditions?
rows.answer: Yes. An AI system intended to be used as a safety component of a lift can qualify as a high-risk AI system, and does so under the Annex I product route rather than the Annex III listed-use route. Under Article 6(1), classification requires both conditions to be fulfilled cumulatively. First, under Article 6(1), point (a), the AI system must be intended to be used as a safety component of a product, or be itself a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I; lifts and safety components for lifts are covered by Directive 2014/33/EU, listed in Annex I, point 4. Second, under Article 6(1), point (b), the lift whose safety component the AI system is must be required to undergo a third-party conformity assessment with a view to its placing on the market or putting into service pursuant to that Directive. Article 6(1) applies irrespective of whether the AI system is placed on the market or put into service independently of the lift. Where so classified, the provider follows the conformity assessment procedure required under Directive 2014/33/EU, with the Chapter III, Section 2 requirements forming part of that assessment (Article 43(3)).
criteria_text: Yes
Condition: AI system intended as safety component of a product covered by Annex I Union harmonisation legislation
Condition: that product (or the AI system itself as a product) required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that legislation
Both conditions cumulative
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states 'Yes' as its first word and maintains that position throughout.
The answer states the AI system must be intended as a safety component of a product covered by Annex I legislation, and specifically references lifts under Directive 2014/33/EU in Annex I, point 4.
The answer states that the product (the lift) must be required to undergo third-party conformity assessment pursuant to the applicable Directive.
The answer explicitly states that both conditions must be fulfilled cumulatively under Article 6(1).

rows.question: Under Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (EU AI Act), how is "risk" defined?
rows.answer: ‘risk’ means the combination of the probability of an occurrence of harm and the severity of that harm;
criteria_text: Combination of probability of occurrence of harm and severity of that harm
criterion_remarks: The candidate answer states the full substance of the definition of 'risk' as set out in Article 3.2, using the exact wording from the regulation.

rows.question: A provider becomes aware of a risk (within the meaning of Article 79(1)) for their high-risk AI system. Does the provider need to take immediate corrective action OR immediately investigate the causes OR both? For example, perhaps it's the market surveillance authority that must investigate the cause, and the provider can help later.
rows.answer: Both duties apply, and both apply immediately and cumulatively to the provider; the market surveillance authority's own investigation does not displace either. Under Article 20(1), a provider that considers or has reason to consider that a high-risk AI system it has placed on the market or put into service is not in conformity must immediately take the necessary corrective actions to bring it into conformity, to withdraw, disable or recall it, as appropriate, and inform the distributors and, where applicable, the deployers, the authorised representative and importers. Under Article 20(2), where the system presents a risk within the meaning of Article 79(1) and the provider becomes aware of that risk, it must immediately investigate the causes, in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable, and inform the competent market surveillance authorities and, where applicable, the notified body that issued the certificate under Article 44, in particular of the nature of the non-compliance and of any relevant corrective action taken. Article 79(2) separately obliges the authority to evaluate and the operator to cooperate; Article 79(4) requires the operator to ensure corrective action for all systems concerned made available on the Union market, failing which Article 79(5) provisional measures follow.
criteria_text: Both
Immediate corrective action required under Article 20(1) where system is non-compliant
Immediate investigation of causes is the provider's own duty under Article 20(2)
Investigation done in collaboration with reporting deployer where applicable, not deferred to market surveillance authority
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states that both duties apply immediately and cumulatively to the provider.
The answer cites Article 20(1) and correctly describes the provider's duty to take immediate corrective action when non-compliance is suspected.
The answer cites Article 20(2) and clearly assigns the immediate investigation of causes to the provider as a distinct obligation.
The answer specifies that the provider must investigate in collaboration with the reporting deployer where applicable, and does not suggest deferral to the market surveillance authority.

rows.question: My local small language model says that, as a distributor of high-risk AI systems, I must be careful that transport conditions do not jeopardize compliance. But AI is just software, isn't it? So I am pretty sure my model hallucinated. What do you say?
rows.answer: The operator's model did not hallucinate. Article 24(3) expressly requires distributors to ensure that, while a high-risk AI system is under their responsibility, storage or transport conditions do not jeopardise the system's compliance with the requirements set out in Section 2. The provision is qualified by "where applicable", which is precisely the concession to the operator's point: where a system is supplied purely as software with no physical carrier, there may be no relevant transport conditions, but where it is embedded in a product, shipped on physical media or hardware, the duty bites. It sits alongside the operator's Article 24(1) duty to verify the CE marking, the EU declaration of conformity and the instructions for use before making the system available, and Article 24(2)'s bar on making a non-conforming system available.

Article 24(3) applies
Duty applies only 'where applicable' (e.g., embedded/supplied hardware or physical media)
criterion_remarks: The answer explicitly states the model did not hallucinate, affirming the correctness of the local model's statement.
The answer cites and explains Article 24(3) as applying to distributors, directly addressing the provision in question.

rows.question: Does the AI Act prohibit or classifies as high-risk the use of AI in drones? Can I use AI in a drone to find who's around in town? And what if it's just a toy drone? And what about toy drones used for other applications?
rows.answer: The AI Act regulates neither drones nor toys as such, only the AI system's intended purpose decides, so there is no drone-specific prohibition or high-risk class. Drone-mounted AI that identifies who is around town is real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces: prohibited where used for law enforcement under Article 5(1)(h), subject only to its exhaustive derogations, targeted search for victims of abduction, trafficking or sexual exploitation and for missing persons (i); prevention of a specific, substantial and imminent threat to life or physical safety, or of a terrorist attack (ii); localisation or identification of a suspect of an Annex II offence punishable by at least four years (iii), with the Article 5(2), (5) authorisation and safeguards. Used by anyone else, it is high-risk under Annex III, point 1(a). A toy drone is treated identically on that route. Separately, Article 6(1) makes it high-risk only if the AI is a safety component of, or itself, a toy covered by Directive 2009/48/EC (Annex I, point 2) and that product must undergo third-party conformity assessment; a toy drone doing something innocuous, with no third-party assessment required, is outside both routes and retains only Article 50(1) disclosure where it interacts directly with persons.
criteria_text: No blanket prohibition/high-risk classification for drones as such — turns on AI system's intended use under Article 6
Drone AI identifying people in public = remote biometric identification, high-risk under Annex III(1)(a), not the 1:1 verification exclusion
Toy status irrelevant — classification depends on intended use, not the device
Toy drone used for other application is high-risk only if that use matches Annex III (or Article 6(1) safety-component/conformity-assessment criteria)
criterion_remarks: States that classification depends on intended use under Article 6, not the drone itself.
Correctly identifies identifying people in town as remote biometric identification under Annex III(1)(a), distinguishes from 1:1 verification.
Explicitly states toy drone is treated the same based on use, not device type.
Explains that toy drone is high-risk only if use falls under Annex III or Article 6(1) criteria, otherwise not.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and well-structured; avoids self-reference and presents information in a coherent, actionable manner.

rows.question: We deployed a high-risk AI system in our company. We have a use in mind that is outside the intended use and our legal team say such a use is definitely no risk (no Annex I nor III apply). Can we just go ahead with the new use and do we need to keep logs for it?
rows.answer: No, you cannot simply go ahead, and yes, the operator must keep the logs. As a deployer the operator is bound by Article 26(1) to use the high‑risk system in accordance with its instructions for use, and a use outside the intended purpose is by definition not covered by them. Under Article 25(1), a deployer that modifies the intended purpose of a high‑risk AI system already placed on the market is thereby considered a provider and assumes the full provider obligations, with the initial provider owing cooperation and technical access under Article 25(2). The operator's legal team's conclusion that neither Annex I nor Annex III is engaged does not de‑classify the system: Annex I (items 1 to 20) classifies through the product and third‑party conformity route under Article 6(1), Annex III through its listed use‑cases under Article 6(2), and the Article 6(3) derogation is a provider self‑assessment documented before placing on the market, not a deployer's post‑deployment judgement. Article 13(3)(b)(iii) confirms that reasonably foreseeable misuse is itself a documented risk dimension. On logging, Article 26(6) requires retention of the automatically generated logs under the operator's control for at least six months. The evidence supplies no text for Articles 10(2), 12(2) or 43(1). So no conclusion is drawn on those provisions here.
criteria_text: No, cannot proceed with the new use
Article 26(1) requires use in accordance with instructions for use; deviating from intended use is not excused merely because that use alone wouldn't trigger Annex III
Yes, logging duty under Article 26(6) still applies regardless of the particular use
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No, you cannot simply go ahead,' which matches the required 'No' verdict for proceeding with the new use.

The answer explains that Article 26(1) binds deployers to use the system in accordance with instructions for use and that a use outside intended purpose is not covered, directly stating the substance of the criterion.
The answer affirms that Article 26(6) requires log retention for at least six months for logs under the operator's control, satisfying the logging obligation regardless of the specific use.

rows.question: Is AI software that helps clinicians take medical decisions around best treatment potentially high-risk? According to what Article and/or Annex?
rows.answer: Yes. Clinical decision-support software recommending treatment is potentially high-risk, and the governing route is Article 6(1) read with point 11 of Annex I (Regulation (EU) 2017/745 on medical devices), not Annex III. Article 6(1) classifies a system as high-risk where both limbs are met: (a) the AI system is itself a product, or a safety component of a product, covered by the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Annex I; and (b) that product must undergo a third-party conformity assessment under that same legislation, which such software does as a Class IIa or higher device. Annex III adds separate routes only for distinct uses, notably Annex III.5(d) emergency triage and Annex III.5(a) public-authority eligibility decisions on healthcare benefits; the Article 6(3) derogation does not reach the Annex I route.
criteria_text: Yes
Article 6(2)
Annex III (healthcare access/provision)

The answer cites Article 6(1), not Article 6(2), and explicitly distinguishes the route from Annex III, contradicting the required criterion.

rows.question: About obligations of transparency to providers who want to use a GPAI model, do you need to disclose: date of release? number of paramaters? applicable model interaction with hardware? license? samples of outlier data used in training? Given clear yes/no to each item.
rows.answer: Yes to the first four, no to the fifth. The governing provision is Article 53(1)(b), which requires information and documentation for providers intending to integrate the model, containing at a minimum the elements in Annex XII. Annex XII.1 expressly lists the date of release and methods of distribution (point (c)); how the model interacts, or can be used to interact, with hardware or software not part of the model itself, where applicable (point (d)); the architecture and number of parameters (point (f)); and the licence for the model (point (h)). Samples of outlier training data are not required: Annex XII.2(c) asks only for the type and provenance of training, testing and validation data and curation methodologies, not data samples.

rows.question: Name the areas of high-risk use cases. Is healthcare decision making one of them?
rows.answer: No, "healthcare decision making" is not itself one of the Annex III areas. Annex III lists eight areas of high-risk use cases: biometrics (Annex III.1); critical infrastructure (Annex III.2); education and vocational training (Annex III.3); employment, workers management and access to self-employment (Annex III.4); access to and enjoyment of essential private services and essential public services and benefits (Annex III.5); law enforcement (Annex III.6); migration, asylum and border control management (Annex III.7); and administration of justice and democratic processes (Annex III.8). A system is high-risk under Article 6(2) only if it falls within a lettered use-case under one of those areas, not merely because it operates in a listed sector. Healthcare appears only as specific use-cases inside area 5: evaluating eligibility of natural persons for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services, and granting, reducing, revoking or reclaiming them (Annex III.5(a)); risk assessment and pricing for life and health insurance (Annex III.5(c)); and emergency call triage and dispatch, including emergency healthcare patient triage systems (Annex III.5(d)). Clinical decision-making software is instead captured, where applicable, by the separate Annex I product route under Article 6(1) as a safety component of a medical device subject to third-party conformity assessment (Annex I.11 to 12).

No
