rows.question: Could the introduction of guardrails in an AI agentic system reduce the risk of the system from high risk to moderate risk? What about changing the capabilities and intended use of the system?
rows.answer: No. Guardrails alone cannot move a system out of high-risk, and the Regulation as adopted has no "moderate risk" tier: classification under Article 6(1) turns on the Annex I product-plus-third-party-conformity-assessment route, and under Article 6(2) on whether the system falls within a listed Annex III use-case, neither test looks at residual risk after mitigation. Guardrails instead operate as risk-control measures under Article 9 and are taken into account when demonstrating compliance with the Section 2 requirements in light of the intended purpose and state of the art (Article 8(1)); they must be reflected in the Annex IV technical documentation, in particular the general description of the system and its design specifications, architecture and computational resources (Annex IV, points 1 and 2), in the Article 12(2) logging traceability (start/stop, input reference data, events relevant to post-market monitoring), and in the instructions for use covering intended purpose, accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity, foreseeable risk circumstances including reasonably foreseeable misuse, explanatory capabilities, performance on specific persons or groups, input-data specifications and output interpretation (Article 13(3)(b)(i), (vii)). Changing capabilities and intended purpose can change classification, since Article 6(2) and the Article 6(3) derogation are purpose-driven, but modifying the intended purpose or making a substantial modification makes that actor a provider under Article 25(1)(b), (c).
criteria_text: No - guardrails alone do not create an intermediate "moderate risk" tier; the Act's Article 6(3) derogation is binary (high-risk or exempted)

Exemption applies only where the system's intended task itself meets one of four Article 6(3) conditions: narrow procedural task; improving a previously completed human activity; detecting deviations from prior decisions without replacing human assessment; or a preparatory task
Yes - changing the system's capabilities/intended use can exit high-risk status if the redefined task now satisfies one of those conditions
Exception: an AI system that performs profiling of natural persons is always high-risk, regardless of guardrails or intended-use changes
criterion_remarks: The answer states that guardrails alone cannot reduce high-risk status and that there is no moderate risk tier, aligning with the binary nature of Article 6(3).

The answer explains that classification depends on the system's intended use and refers to the purpose-driven nature of Article 6(2) and (3), implying that only a change in task meeting the listed conditions can affect classification.

The answer confirms that changing capabilities and intended purpose can change classification, which matches the criterion, noting that such changes are governed by the purpose-driven tests in Article 6.

Although not explicitly mentioned, the answer does not contradict the profiling exception and correctly frames high-risk status as tied to use-case and purpose, leaving room for the profiling exception to apply; it does not assert that changing purpose can override all high-risk classifications, thus not violating the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, third-person, regulatory register; well-structured and coherent, with precise references to provisions without self-reference or hedging.

rows.question: Is the use of deep-fake images in university classes to represent e.g. skin conditions in patients allowed? Does the artificial nature of the content need to be disclosed for such an evidently educational and illustrative use? If so, does the lighter transparency requirement apply like for certain law enforcement situations?
rows.answer: Yes, such use is permitted: generating synthetic images of skin conditions for teaching is not among the practices prohibited by Article 5(1), and the classroom use you describe does not fall within any Annex III listed use-case. Disclosure is nonetheless required. As deployer of an AI system that generates or manipulates image content constituting a deep fake, the university must disclose that the content has been artificially generated or manipulated (Article 50(4), first subparagraph). The only exemption from that duty is where the use is authorised by law to detect, prevent, investigate or prosecute criminal offences; an educational institution cannot invoke it. The lighter regime does not apply. The limitation to "disclosure of the existence of such generated or manipulated content in an appropriate manner that does not hamper the display or enjoyment of the work" is confined to content forming part of an evidently artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work or programme, clinical illustration is none of these. The human-review/editorial-responsibility exemption concerns only artificially generated text published to inform the public on matters of public interest. Separately, the provider must mark the outputs in a machine-readable, detectable format (Article 50(2)).
criteria_text: Yes, permitted
Disclosure still required under Article 50(4)
Lighter regime applies as "analogous work" to artistic/creative/fictional content — only existence of generated content must be disclosed, without hampering display/enjoyment
Law-enforcement carve-out is a full exemption, not a lighter regime, and is inapplicable here
criterion_remarks: The answer states that generating synthetic images for teaching is not prohibited and does not fall under Annex III, affirming permissibility.
The answer explicitly states that disclosure is required under Article 50(4), first subparagraph, for deep fake image generation by deployers.

The answer rejects the applicability of the lighter regime, stating that clinical illustration does not qualify as an artistic, creative, satirical, fictional or analogous work, contrary to the criterion which asserts the lighter regime does apply.
The answer correctly distinguishes the law-enforcement exemption as a full exemption that does not apply here, and notes it is inapplicable to educational use.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality.

rows.question: A supermarket uses an AI tool that analyzes only current-cart and checkout anomalies (no biometrics, no face recognition, no sensitive-trait inference, no cross-context social scoring) to flag transactions for optional manual bag checks by store staff. The retailer claims this is "high risk like policing", as it: resembles investigation of potentially criminal offences (theft) + evaluates or classifies persons based on observed behaviour in a way that may lead to detrimental or unfavourable treatment. Is this situation potentially high-risk?
rows.answer: No. On these facts the tool is neither prohibited nor high-risk. Article 5(1)(d) bans AI that predicts the risk of a natural person committing a criminal offence based solely on profiling or personality traits, but expressly does not apply to systems supporting human assessment of involvement in criminal activity already based on objective and verifiable facts directly linked to that activity, current-cart and checkout anomalies are such facts, and the bag check is an optional human decision. Article 5(1)(c) is not engaged either: there is no evaluation over a certain period of time producing a social score, no detrimental treatment in unrelated social contexts (Article 5(1)(c)(i)), and none disproportionate to the behaviour (Article 5(1)(c)(ii)). High-risk status would require a listed Annex III use-case; the law-enforcement entries cover law enforcement authorities, not a retailer's own loss prevention.
criteria_text: No
Annex III.6 categories apply only where the AI system is used by or on behalf of law enforcement authorities (or by Union institutions/bodies in support of law enforcement authorities)

A supermarket's own loss-prevention/bag-check tool, run by store staff, is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, so it falls outside Annex III.6 regardless of its resemblance to investigative or evaluative functions
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No' as the position, which matches the required verdict.

The answer states that the law-enforcement entries in Annex III cover law enforcement authorities, not a retailer's own loss prevention, which conveys the substance that Annex III.6 applies only to systems used by or on behalf of law enforcement.

The answer explicitly distinguishes the supermarket's tool from Annex III.6 by stating it is not used by or on behalf of a law enforcement authority, and clarifies that the tool falls outside Annex III.6 despite functional resemblance.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents reasoning in a logical, actionable manner.

rows.question: We developed a product listed in Annex I where an AI system is a safety component. We had the option to opt out of the third-party conformity assessment base case by using harmonized standards. Thus no third-party conformity assessment happened. This means we can skip the requirements of Chapter 3 Section 2 of the AI Act, right?
rows.answer: No, you cannot skip Chapter III, Section 2. Article 43(3), final subparagraph, allows a manufacturer to use a sectoral opt-out from third-party conformity assessment only if it has also applied harmonised standards or, where applicable, the common specifications referred to in Article 41, covering all requirements set out in Section 2 of that Chapter. The opt-out changes the route for demonstrating conformity, not the substance: the Section 2 requirements continue to apply and form part of the assessment under the relevant Section A Annex I act. The system remains high-risk under Article 6(1) as a safety component of a product covered by the acts listed in machinery, toys, recreational craft, lifts, ATEX equipment, radio equipment, pressure equipment, cableways, personal protective equipment, gas appliances, medical devices, in vitro diagnostics, civil aviation security, two- and three-wheel vehicles, agricultural and forestry vehicles, marine equipment, rail interoperability, motor vehicle type-approval, general vehicle safety, and civil aviation. Article 43(1), points (a) to (d), governs only Annex III point 1 systems and is not the operator's route. The supplied evidence contains no text for Article 41(1)(a)(i), (iv), so those limbs cannot be stated.
criteria_text: No
Section 2 requirements still apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment (Art. 43(3), second sentence)
The third-party opt-out under sectoral legislation is available only if harmonised standards/common specifications applied cover ALL Section 2 requirements, not just the sectoral ones
criterion_remarks: The answer clearly states 'No, you cannot skip Chapter III, Section 2', which matches the required 'No' verdict.
The answer explains that the Section 2 requirements continue to apply and form part of the sectoral conformity assessment, citing the relevant provision and substance.

The answer specifies that the opt-out is available only if harmonised standards or common specifications cover all Section 2 requirements, not just the sectoral ones, directly reflecting the criterion.
rows.tone_remark: Professional, neutral, and structured in clear prose without self-reference, hedging, or informality; presents information in a way usable by a compliance professional.
